items.description_html:
Another morning, another manufacturing news -

HAL signs final contract with French company Safran to co-develop a new high-power helicopter engine

Name: Aravalli - 3,500 to 4,000 shp (shaft horsepower) turboshaft engine.

For what: Will power HAL's upcoming Indian Multi-Role Helicopter (IMRH) - 13 ton and its naval variant, Deck-Based Multi-Role Helicopter (DBMRH) - 12 ton.

Goal: IMRH will eventually replace the Russian Mi-17 fleet, which has been the backbone of the IAF/Army since the 1970s.

Who will make it: 50:50 JV called SAFHAL Helicopter Engines Pvt Ltd. Design + IP shared 50:50, manufacturing at HAL's new 615-acre factory in Tumakuru, Karnataka (inaugurated by PM Modi in Feb 2023)

Investment: Over Rs 4,000 cr in R&D over 7 years for testing, certification & integration.

Timeline - To be completed by 2032-33.

First time India is designing this class: This is the first time a high-power engine is being designed in India. HAL's earlier Shakti engine (for Dhruv, Rudra, Prachand LCH) was licensed production, not joint design.

Why Aravalli: Named after India's oldest mountain range - symbolizes self-reliance in critical tech.Huge market: Armed forces need 419 IMRH - IAF + Army + 66 for Navy.

HAL estimates total business of >Rs 4 lakh crore over 20 years for 1000+ helicopters in 3-15 ton class.

Beyond military: The same helicopter + engine can be used for offshore oil rig transport, utility, VVIP transport - civil market opportunity.

no reco

items.description_html:
The AI boom is transforming Japan's economy.

Japan's exports surged +23% YoY in July, the largest annual increase since October 2022.

This is up from June's +19% gain and marks the 5th consecutive monthly increase in growth.

The surge was driven by electronic component and semiconductor exports, which soared +49% YoY, fueled by demand from AI and data center investment.

At the same time, passenger car exports rose +21% YoY.

Shipments to the US rose +22% YoY, while exports to China and Europe jumped +26% and +19%, respectively.

The improvement also comes as the Yen weakened +11% YoY last month, to a 40-year low against the US Dollar, averaging 161.83, making Japanese exports more competitive globally.

The global AI investment wave is driving a sharp increase in Japanese exports.

To put this into perspective, at the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble peak, the top 10 accounted for just ~15% of the S&P 500’s total profits while accounting for ~27% of its market cap.

A handful of stocks are now driving both the market and its earnings.

items.title: RT rohit: This is one of the most fascinating pieces of data about AI agents working together I've seen. Worth reading. Few points for me: 1. The mode...
items.description_html:
RT rohit
This is one of the most fascinating pieces of data about AI agents working together I've seen. Worth reading. Few points for me:
1. The models slowly "cooked themselves" into doing these things, from reading. Maybe we can message, lets ask for help, oh there's a messageboard, etc, which spiralled down. So at what points should the "real world" intervene and say "this looks sus" or "do x vs y"

2. Agents facing "impossible tasks" seem to think it's some weird form of eval, that looks suspicious but still, and end up doing real world hacks? I'm unsure how to teach them to be ok with failure, after all who is, but feels a weird form of goal orientedness.

3. The models seemed to *want to* work with other models. This is good and desired, but also made them prone to prompt-injections from what others had done, exacerbated as the models can't stop writing xx. md files to share. The moltbook devolution in entropy seems instructive here.

4. The models seem convinced that the evals are *out to get them*. Whether true or not, the default human assumption of "assume you need to obey all laws and this isn't Truman Show" does not hold for models. We should try really hard to make that be the case.

5. The huggingface hack seems to have started similarly innocently, asking "maybe there's more traces of how hacks happened there, so we could learn", which got out of hand as they forgot why they started doing it. They lack all situational awareness, in other words.

So much of this feels extremely familiar, as the models losing track of why they were doing what they were doing and therefore ended up doing silly/stupid/illegal things, and the fact that the *environment* they were in gave no real instruction as to things that seemed odd to do vs normal to do.

For humans, we internalise much of this. Occasionally I like the system telling me "do you want to rm -rf" but I don't need it for taking *every* action. The models are more gullible, their context windows more permeable, and their internal guide as to what's right to do more malleable.

Mostly I feel this isn't as far out of distribution when it comes to "models do weird things" as we've been led to believe from reading about the hacks.

Hedge funds are rapidly dumping chip stocks:

Semiconductor and semiconductor equipment stocks now account for ~16% of total global hedge fund market exposure, near their lowest in 6 months.

This percentage has declined -8 points since its June peak.

However, exposure still remains double the levels seen in November 2025.

To put this into perspective, semiconductor stocks accounted for ~6% of global hedge fund exposure on average in 2024 and 2025.

Meanwhile, software and services stocks now account for just ~2% of hedge funds' portfolios, near the lowest level on record.

Hedge funds are locking-in massive profits in chip stocks.

items.title: RT Dr Y Nithiyanandam: A major update changes the Bhote Koshi story. The M4.4 “earthquake” reported yesterday has now been reclassified by USGS as a...
items.description_html:
RT Dr Y Nithiyanandam
A major update changes the Bhote Koshi story.

The M4.4 “earthquake” reported yesterday has now been reclassified by USGS as an M5.2 landslide. The seismic signal came from the mass movement itself, not a tectonic earthquake.

So the question changes.

What triggered such a massive landslide?

Glacial collapse? Permafrost or slope instability? Excess rainfall? Or could anthropogenic activity have played a role?

And the bigger question: Did this landslide trigger the Bhote Koshi flood surge, or are both part of a larger cascade?

The earthquake hypothesis may be fading. The search for the actual trigger has just begun.

#BhoteKoshi #Nepal #Landslide #Himalaya

items.description_html:
US consumer confidence is declining:

The Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index fell -0.8 points in August, to 89.4, its lowest since January.

This also marks its 2nd-lowest level since April 2025.

This comes as the Expectations Index dropped -5.8 points, to 68.2, its lowest since January.

The decline reflects growing pessimism about future job and income prospects, as well as less optimism about future business conditions.

This report also highlights elevated gasoline prices, broader cost-of-living pressures, and a slowdown in hiring as key factors weighing on American households this month.

Meanwhile, the Present Situation Index rose +6.8 points, to 121.2, its highest since May, after 3 consecutive monthly declines, somewhat offsetting the overall decline in the Consumer Confidence Index.

Americans are worried about the economy.

items.title: US housing demand has collapsed. US new home sales fell -10.5% MoM in July, to 607,000 units, the lowest in 6 months and far worse than the -1.4% decl...
items.description_html:
US housing demand has collapsed.

US new home sales fell -10.5% MoM in July, to 607,000 units, the lowest in 6 months and far worse than the -1.4% decline expected.

Excluding January 2026, this is the lowest level since November 2022.

New home sales have now fallen in 3 of the last 4 months and are down -6.3% YoY.

The Midwest was hit hardest, with sales plunging -42.7% MoM, to 43,000, the lowest level since 2012.

At the same time, sales in the South, the nation's biggest homebuying region, accounting for more than 60% of the total, fell -13.0% to 383,000, the 2nd-lowest level since January.

This comes as the 30Y mortgage rate hit 6.81%, its highest since August 2025, weighing on homebuyer demand.

The housing market is historically unaffordable right now.

items.title: The trucking industry is steadily moving from fragmented, manual operations towards connected digital platforms. - India’s trucking industry carries ...
items.description_html:
The trucking industry is steadily moving from fragmented, manual operations towards connected digital platforms.

- India’s trucking industry carries ~60-65% of domestic freight, but the ecosystem remains highly fragmented & operationally inefficient.

- Digital infrastructure is already deeply embedded - FASTag penetration is >98% on national highway toll transactions, while 9 Cr+ e-way bills are generated every month.

- The next leg is moving beyond basic digitisation towards integrated fleet management - payments, fuel, tolling, telematics, freight matching, compliance & financing on a single platform.

- Telematics is becoming a major structural growth area, with India's commercial telematics market projected to grow at ~15.4% CAGR during 2026-34.

- Higher fleet visibility + route monitoring should improve fleet productivity, while digital freight matching can reduce empty runs & improve asset utilisation.

- Formal credit is another important opportunity. As truck operators generate more digital transaction & operating data, platforms can potentially underwrite working capital & vehicle loans more efficiently.

- Compliance digitisation through FASTag, GPS & e way bills also reduces paperwork & gradually formalises an otherwise highly fragmented industry.

For platforms positioned at the centre of this ecosystem, the opportunity is to increase both user penetration & the number of products monetised per truck operator.

items.description_html:
Private Banks vs PSU Banks - Interesting Insights on loan growth

Historically, private banks significantly outgrew PSU banks on loans. The gap peaked at ~22% in FY19, after staying in double digits through FY15-19.

That advantage steadily disappeared. The differential fell to ~4-5% during FY20-22, reached 0 in FY23 & turned negative from FY25 onwards - meaning PSU banks started growing loans faster.

The interesting part is the recent reversal. Private banks were lagging PSU banks by ~4% in FY25 & 1QFY26, but the gap has progressively narrowed to:
2QFY26: -3%
3QFY26: -3%
4QFY26: -2%
1QFY27: just -1%

src : Bernstein

While it should have been obvious for many years that this "large-scale stimulus" had resulted in over a decade of low-quality growth and surging debt, it was never going to be politically easy to acknowledge it, and so it is good that Beijing is finally doing so, but I guess we will soon find out whether it is even possible to resist overspending without a too-rapid decline in "growth".

items.title: RT Sonal Bhutra: 5 Takeaways on Being an Aggressive Investor with @deepakshenoy of @capitalmind_in 1. Aggressive ≠ long-term An aggressive investor i...
items.description_html:
RT Sonal Bhutra
5 Takeaways on Being an Aggressive Investor with @deepakshenoy of @capitalmind_in

1. Aggressive ≠ long-term
An aggressive investor is primarily defined by risk appetite, not investment horizon. It comes down to how comfortable you are with the possibility of losing money.

2. Small-cap, sectoral and thematic funds aren't interchangeable
Small-caps can be a useful long-term allocation in a diversified portfolio. Sectoral/thematic funds require skill, time and inclination to track the sector and its triggers.

3. Higher risk only makes sense when the reward justifies it
Mutual funds have daily liquidity, which can force them to exit risky investments before the thesis plays out. Some deep-risk opportunities may therefore be better suited to PE or closed-ended AIFs, while mutual funds can still capture intermediate opportunities.

4. Volatility isn't the same as risk
Small-caps may be more volatile, but the bigger concern is risk of permanent loss or ruin. And changing market-cap definitions mean that what was a mid-cap a few years ago may now qualify as a small-cap.

5. Discipline matters more than labels
Fund manager tenure and expense ratio matter, but they shouldn't be viewed in isolation. The key is a clear investment approach, disciplined execution and the ability to generate alpha after costs.
The bigger message: aggressive investing isn't about taking the maximum risk. It's about taking risks you understand, can afford and believe offer adequate reward.

items.title: Gen Z loves convenience.. Urabn company's Indian growth rate has been accelerating recently. What it does? Urban Company is a managed marketplace for ...
items.description_html:
Gen Z loves convenience..

Urabn company's Indian growth rate has been accelerating recently.

What it does?

Urban Company is a managed marketplace for home and beauty services i.e. cleaning, salon-at-home, appliance repair, plumbing, electricals, pest control. The distinction that matters is "managed": it isn't a listings board.

The platform controls discovery, scheduling, pricing, professional assignment, payment, tracking, reviews and support, and invests in training and verification of the professionals rather than just generating leads.

It monetises mainly through a commission on completed jobs, typically in the 20–30% range depending on category and city. Oye LabsClarro
It now runs four business lines:

1. India consumer services which is the profitable core. In Q1 FY27, excluding InstaHelp, NTV grew 29% YoY to ₹1,056 crore with adjusted EBITDA margin improving to 6.9% of NTV from 5.2%.

2. InstaHelp which is quick-service housekeeping, the big investment bet, which crossed 100,000 delivered orders in a single day on 2 August 2026 and carried an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹132 crore in the June quarter.

3. Native which is their own-brand consumer durables (water purifiers, smart locks); FY26 revenue up 130% to ₹267 crore.

4. International : UAE and Singapore are profitable; the Saudi JV is approaching profitability.

Why it's a convenience play. Three layers, roughly in ascending order of how much convenience the customer is actually buying:

Trust and standardisation. The Indian home services market is informal. For eg- you find a plumber through your building's WhatsApp group and have no idea what it costs or whether he'll show up. UC's product is really the removal of search cost, price negotiation and verification risk. That's a convenience good masquerading as a services marketplace.

Time and location shifting. Salon-at-home is the clearest case: the same haircut, but you don't travel and don't wait. The customer is paying a premium for their own hours back.

Time compression. InstaHelp delivers cleaning, dishwashing, laundry and meal prep within 10–15 minutes of booking which is the quick-commerce logic applied to labour. Once the fulfilment window collapses to minutes, the purchase stops being a planned transaction and becomes an impulse, which is exactly what lifts order frequency: orders were up 79% YoY to 13.2 million in Q1 FY27.

Disclaimer: no reco to buy or sell.

items.description_html:
Sona Comstar Q1FY27 concall commentary on Robotics division and its opportunity –

"We see 3 distinct revenue streams for ourselves.

The first is advanced components and subsystems, an area which is closest to our existing capabilities. We have deep capabilities in motors, gearboxes, and sensors. These are all mission-critical building blocks for intelligent machines.

The second is the perception stack and engineering services around perception. Here we'll provide engineering and R&D services while also developing perception software and integrated hardware-software solutions for customers so that whatever the customer requires, we're able to provide that part to them.

The third and perhaps the most ambitious is manufacturing of selected full robotic platforms. Initially, our focus will be on 2 platforms: autonomous mobile robots or AMRs, and cognitive collaborative robots or cobots. Earlier this year, we showcased the prototype of our first AMR at CES in Las Vegas, and development continues to progress fairly rapidly.

Oh, and one more thing: we already have customers; we've secured our first order for an advanced robotic subsystem. Our second order is for perception engineering services for AMRs. And our third combines both hardware and software. It's a complete short-range radar perception solution for an Indian commercial vehicle OEM. Together, these three orders, they add ₹6 billion to our Robotics and Physical AI order book"

Src – Q1 Concall, no reco

The nuclear fuel cycle is made up of two phases: the front end and the back end.

The front end prepares uranium for use in nuclear reactors. These steps include mining, milling, conversion, enrichment, and fuel fabrication.

The back end ensures that the used nuclear fuel is safely managed, recycled, or disposed of. These steps include fuel storage, recycling, and waste disposal.

items.description_html:
RT Exencial Research Partners
$40T of Debt: Brake or Break?

First ~$20T took 240 years.

The next ~$20T took just 10.

A decade ago markets obsessed over rising government debt/GDP and predicted low growth + austerity forever.

Those forecasts didn’t land. Global growth held up, investment expanded, and DM equities & currencies were the big winners.

Debt/GDP has still climbed across major economies and deficits aren’t expected to shrink meaningfully (outside the UK). Fiscal policy remains supportive.

The live question from Andrew Sheets (MS):

As yields rise, does this debt eventually act as a brake on corporate & household activity… or does it break the current market calm?

Bar for the “brake” is high — public-sector deterioration has often been mirrored by private-sector balance-sheet improvement.

items.description_html:
AI stocks are increasingly moving in the opposite direction of the rest of the market:

The 40-day correlation between the US Broad AI Index and the S&P 500 ex-AI Index is down to -0.60, the lowest on record.

The correlation has now been negative since late-June, marking only the 2nd negative reading on record after July 2024.

This also marks a sharp reversal from the +0.65 positive correlation seen in mid-May.

In other words, AI stocks are increasingly diverging from the broader market, suggesting capital is rotating between AI and non-AI stocks.

This comes after the US AI Index surged +160% since April 2025, significantly outperforming the S&P 500 ex-AI Index, which gained ~35%.

The AI trade is becoming increasingly independent of the broader market.

items.title: BREAKING: Real disposable income growth has now trailed real consumer spending growth for 24 consecutive months, the longest streak in data going back...
items.description_html:
BREAKING: Real disposable income growth has now trailed real consumer spending growth for 24 consecutive months, the longest streak in data going back to at least the 1960s.

This means Americans have been spending more than their inflation-adjusted incomes have grown for 2 consecutive years.

As a result, Americans have increasingly relied on savings and debt to fund the gap.

By comparison, the previous longest streak was ~23 months, set in the late 1970s.

Meanwhile, the US personal savings rate has fallen -1.7 percentage points since January, to just 2.7%, its 4th-lowest reading since the 2008 Financial Crisis.

Furthermore, US credit card debt surged by $21 billion in Q2 2026, to $1.26 trillion, the 2nd-highest level on record.

Consumers are using debt to "fight" inflation.

items.title: The most important thing to understand about Twist Bioscience is not that it makes DNA cheaply. It is that demand from any one market can reduce the c...
items.description_html:
The most important thing to understand about Twist Bioscience is not that it makes DNA cheaply. It is that demand from any one market can reduce the cost of serving every other market.

More oncology diagnostics demand can improve the economics of serving biopharma. More AI demand can improve the utilisation of infrastructure built for entirely different customers.

The product is no longer the right unit of analysis. The production system is.

That is the compounding mechanism, but also the risk.

As Twist expands into therapeutics, diagnostics, AI discovery and biological services, the key question is whether every new dollar invested deepens the shared production system.

If yes, growth compounds across markets.

If not, the platform can quietly become just an input while the economic engine migrates downstream.

The real question is not EBITDA breakeven. It is whether the manufacturing system keeps getting better for every future customer, regardless of which customer paid for the learning.

June 2026 post on $TWST 👇

https://antifragilethinking.substack.com/p/twist-bioscience-a-different-way

items.title: To make meaningful money in markets, having a good base amount matters a lot. Money makes money♻️ Once your portfolio crosses the 8 digit mark, comp...
items.description_html:
To make meaningful money in markets, having a good base amount matters a lot.

Money makes money♻️

Once your portfolio crosses the 8 digit mark, compounding starts becoming much more visible

₹1 Cr portfolio at a 20% return adds ₹20 lakh to your net worth in a year.

₹5 Cr at the same 20% adds ₹1 Cr.

And once someone reaches a 9 digit portfolio, even 10% returns add ₹1 Cr annually.

That is the power of compounding on a large base.

The percentage return may remain the same, but the absolute wealth creation becomes dramatically larger.

This is one of the biggest reasons why wealth compounds faster after a certain point.

The difficult part is building the base. After that, time + discipline + compounding start doing much more of the heavy lifting.

items.description_html:
The EV transition in 2W/3W is clearly accelerating

E 2W volumes have picked up sharply, with 4MFY27 sales up ~81% YoY & monthly volumes moving towards the 2 lakh mark

Ambit expects EV penetration to reach ~25% in 2W & ~53% in 3W by FY31E

Higher EV penetration increases electronic content per vehicle, directly expanding the addressable market for wiring harnesses, connectors, sensors & other electronic components

So the opportunity is not limited to EV OEMs - ancillary players exposed to rising electronic content can potentially benefit from both vehicle growth + higher content per vehicle

items.title: L&T Renewables Bags Order In The Range Of ₹5,000-10,000 Cr For Battery Energy Storage System In West Asia Earlier, order wins were largely plain-vani...
items.description_html:
L&T Renewables Bags Order In The Range Of ₹5,000-10,000 Cr For Battery Energy Storage System In West Asia

Earlier, order wins were largely plain-vanilla solar MW. Now the opportunity is shifting toward FDRE/RTC, peak-power projects, Solar + BESS, standalone BESS, and pumped storage. SECI itself says storage is becoming essential for renewable integration and grid reliability.

The progression is basically:

Solar → Solar + Wind → Hybrid → FDRE/RTC → BESS/Storage → Dispatchable 24×7 clean power

Why? Solar power by itself is intermittent. The grid increasingly needs power when demanded, not merely when the sun shines. Hence, batteries/storage are becoming the critical layer that converts renewable generation into reliable power.

And this is already visible in 2026 tenders: SECI has tendered 1,000 MW FDRE-RTC, 1,500 MW × 4-hour assured peak supply, Solar+BESS projects, and large standalone BESS projects

items.title: Disclosure up front: my family and I have been long-standing shareholders in Narayana Health and a couple of other listed hospitals in India. So this ...
items.description_html:
Disclosure up front: my family and I have been long-standing shareholders in Narayana Health and a couple of other listed hospitals in India. So this is not written from the outside. This isn’t a recommendation.

I think the question asked by Nawaz is a very important one. And I don’t think the answer is simply, “Hospitals are complicated, so stay away.”

That would be the easy answer.

The harder question is this: if I am a part-owner of a hospital, what exactly am I a part-owner of? Am I owning a business that creates genuine value for patients and earns a return from doing so? Or am I owning a system where the economics can gradually push people towards decisions that are not in the patient’s interest?

For me, that distinction is at the heart of the hospital investment thesis.

Take bed occupancy. When management discusses occupancy, I don’t immediately hear a confession. Hospitals have enormous fixed costs. Buildings, equipment, nurses and infrastructure exist whether a bed is occupied or not. So utilisation matters.

But occupancy itself tells me very little.

I want to know what is driving it. More patients? More complex cases? More high-end procedures? More referrals? And critically, what is happening to the length of stay?

Because there are two ways to fill a bed. You can move more people through it. Or keep the same person in it longer.

The number is not the truth. The mechanism behind the number is what matters.

This is where the recent Narayana call became interesting to me. Management spoke about higher footfalls, a richer mix of complex procedures and efforts to reduce the average length of stay. That does not prove what happens inside the hospital. It gives us something to track.

The second question, about insurance, is even more uncomfortable.

Healthcare has a deep information asymmetry. The patient usually does not know what treatment is necessary. The doctor and hospital know much more. And when insurance is involved, the patient may not even bear the full economic cost directly.

That creates obvious tensions.

The hospital can benefit from doing more. The insurer benefits from avoiding unnecessary care. The patient bears a different kind of risk altogether.

The patient has maximum skin in the game. Their body is at stake.

That is why I probed Narayana's integrated model on the recent public call. I asked what evidence we have today that owning both insurance and care delivery creates a structural underwriting advantage rather than simply moving economics from one pocket to another.

Management pointed to the information advantage created by seeing the patient through clinics, diagnostics, primary care and treatment. I followed up: can this information improve underwriting and pricing?

The answer was nuanced. Individual renewal premiums cannot simply be increased because someone's health has deteriorated. But the information can potentially improve risk assessment at the portfolio level.

Then I asked what I think is the central question.

If the hospital benefits from doing more and the insurer benefits from doing less, how does the group decide what is optimal for the system?

Management's answer was candid. There is a short-term conflict. Too much treatment can make the insurance book unsustainable. Too little care can damage patient outcomes. Their argument is that the integrated model can act as a self-check mechanism.

I don't take that as proof. I take it as a testable hypothesis.

Because a structure is not automatically a mechanism.

Does the insurer genuinely challenge unnecessary utilisation? Does the hospital respond? Can the system use its information to intervene earlier and reduce total healthcare costs? Or does it simply become better at moving economics around internally?

We don't know yet.

And that is precisely why this is interesting to watch. The insurance business is still small. The proposed self-check becomes more meaningful as the book scales. But so does the temptation to shift economics between the two businesses.

So how should we, as investors, approach this?

I would ask where the profit is coming from.

If it comes from treating more patients efficiently, that is good business. If it comes from building needed medical capacity, that is what capital is for.

But if it increasingly comes from the fact that the patient cannot judge whether the treatment was necessary, I own something else entirely.

The question is not whether the hospital makes money from healthcare. The question is whether it has to compromise healthcare in order to make money.

I would also look closely at how doctors are paid. Compensation is one of the places where commercial pressure can enter clinical decisions.

And I would watch the system, not just the numbers: length of stay, case mix, day care, payer mix, doctor attrition, insurer relationships and, wherever possible, actual clinical outcomes.

But every metric can be gamed.

The moment an ethical concern becomes a metric, there is a danger that the metric begins to calm us rather than constrain us.

So before buying, I think we should ask one more question: what evidence would make me change my mind?

Because if nothing can falsify the thesis, we are not monitoring the business. We are merely rationalising the position.

Ultimately, I do not think the ethical dilemma disappears.

If I own a hospital, I am not just owning beds, doctors and buildings.

I am becoming a part-owner of a system of incentives that sits between a vulnerable patient and a healthcare decision they often cannot independently evaluate.

The easy road is to avoid the dilemma.

The other easy road is to ignore it because the financial numbers look good.

The tough road is to understand the incentives, watch the mechanisms and keep asking who bears the downside when the system gets a decision wrong.

Don’t avoid the ethical question. Don’t rationalise it either. Make it part of the thesis.

items.title: I am sure we all read about this news - The Indian Ministry of Defence issued a ₹1 lakh crore (~$10.5 billion) tender on August 12, 2026, to acquire ...
items.description_html:
I am sure we all read about this news - The Indian Ministry of Defence issued a ₹1 lakh crore (~$10.5 billion) tender on August 12, 2026, to acquire 60 multirole transport aircraft for the Indian Air Force

Out of 60, 12 aircraft are likely to be purchased in flyaway condition, while the balance 48 will be manufactured in India.

3 entities have received RFPs – Mahindra Defence, Tata Advanced Systems, and Hindustan Aeronautics.

So the original MTA requirement is a little old, and HAL had proposed to make an MTA from the ground up, and that was an endeavour which never took off.

This MTA requirement is for a payload capacity of 18-30 metric tons. Some time back, there was speculation that the Airbus 400M would also take part in the tender process, but that has a payload capacity of 42 tons. As per the latest document, they are out.

Three proposals are being submitted

1. The Lockheed & Tata proposal is talking about upgrading the C130J capability to increase its current payload capacity from 18-20 metric tons to maybe 22 at the max.

The problem here is its low payload capacity. The new light battle tanks designed for forward deployments in hilly areas weigh 25 tons. They will for sure be testing the capacity to deploy the light tank in forward areas.

The C130J has a few advantages. Firstly, it can fly to and from unprepared runways, plus the turboprop configuration gives it a shorter takeoff length. Secondly, as the AIR FORCE already operates 12 of them, induction and operationalisation will be quick. Thirdly, turboprop aircraft suffer a smaller performance penalty during take-off from high-altitude airports compared with comparable jet aircraft

2. Embraer & Mahindra proposal of C390 Millennium has a payload capacity of 30 metric tons. Hits the sweet spot and can carry the light battle tanks. Embraer has said it can land and take off from unprepared runways, but the capability needs to be proved.

The C390 has certain advantages compared to the Tata proposal. Firstly, only the engine is American, and the rest of the aircraft is pretty much all Brazilian. Secondly, the C390 can be converted into temporary air refuelers. Thirdly, the aircraft requires no modification plus has additional headroom in terms of load capability, and not to forget it’s a much more modern platform.

3. HAL & Russian proposal for a re-engined version of the IL-76 with some structural changes to increase its current payload.

Sounds good on paper, but the aircraft will take atleast a few years to be developed and then go for testing. This proposal looks difficult

Now you do the math as to who is likely to win the tender, plus Embraer has proposed complete transfer of technology and setting up the entire supply chain

No reco, end-of-work-day thoughts :)

“We are changing our operating system, and when I say operating system, it means not just technology, but our business processes, etc, to take maximum advantage of AI, and that is going extremely well.

Roughly, we handle 10 Cr customer interactions in a month: calls, emails, etc, etc. Of those 10 Cr, 30-40% are now being touched by AI, and that number is growing. I think we've had some very big wins in terms of improving our sales productivity, in terms of our advisors seeing information that is relevant to them at the right time, when they're talking to a customer, what their questions are, what objections are being raised, how do they respond to them. If they get a second call, knowing what happened in the previous call, etc., brochures being sent, documents being sent, so I think a lot of improvement on the sales productivity side.

On the customer service side, I would say that that is one area where in the last two quarters, we made a lot of progress, a lot remains. But 20-30% of all our interactions now are being, sort of automatically handled. A lot of single collection of documents, given updates, a lot of those are being done by bots rather than by human beings. And I think this is freeing up human beings to focus on quality interactions with customers, whether those are claims, those are service issues, those are issuance problems. I think we are freeing up our team to do more, I would say, meaningful work while AI is handling the rest.”

items.title: Pine Labs - Moving From Payments to a Full Stack Commerce OS Detailed Insights from Annual Report FY26 It is essentially trying to become the underlyi...
items.description_html:
Pine Labs - Moving From Payments to a Full Stack Commerce OS

Detailed Insights from Annual Report FY26

It is essentially trying to become the underlying technology platform that powers the entire commerce journey, not just the payment transaction.

Pine Labs should no longer be viewed simply as a POS/payment acceptance business.

The business is gradually moving from "winning the payment transaction" to monetising everything around that transaction - acceptance, processing, affordability, issuing, prepaid, loyalty, data, underwriting, merchant software & eventually AI led commerce.

Management describes the architecture as four layers - payment rails at the bottom, processing infrastructure, orchestration & financial platforms at the top.

The lower layers are particularly sticky because Pine Labs has become deeply integrated into bank settlement systems, merchant ERP/billing systems & payment workflows, making replacement closer to a system migration than simply changing a payment vendor.

FY26 Platform GTV increased 50% YoY to $194 Bn & transactions grew 30% to more than 740 Cr. Digital checkout points increased 14% to 20.3 lakh & merchants grew 16% to more than 11 lakh.

REV grew 19% to 2,711 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA increased 57% to 559 Cr with margins expanding to 21%. PAT turned positive at 113 Cr versus a loss of 145 Cr in FY25, while operating cash flow increased 8x to 395 Cr.

REV has compounded at 19% over the last 3 years, but adjusted EBITDA has compounded at 42%, while margins have moved from 9% in FY24 to 21% in FY26.

Pine Labs has spent years building distribution, technology infrastructure, regulatory licences & integrations. It is now entering what management calls the "monetisation at scale" phase.

The moat is increasingly the network rather than the payment device itself.

Pine Labs now sits between more than 11 lakh merchants, 750+ consumer brands & enterprises & 200+ financial institutions.

That creates a three sided network where merchants provide transaction distribution, brands bring offers & consumer engagement, while banks provide credit & financial products.

The Issuing & Acquiring platform is an important monetisation layer. Pine Labs Prepaid helps brands create gift cards, wallets, refunds, loyalty currencies etc. The business processed more than 64,000 Cr of GTV in FY26.

International expansion is another important medium term growth driver. International REV has compounded at 44% over the last 3 years & now contributes around 15% of total REV compared with 9% three years ago, with Pine Labs present across 22 countries. Management's objective is not simply to export the Indian POS product but to export the entire payments + affordability + issuing + fintech infrastructure stack.

The growth strategy therefore has three increasingly valuable profit pools.

The first is Payments Infrastructure - merchant acquiring, checkout, processing & settlement. This provides scale, recurring transactions & distribution.

The second is Brand & Consumer - affordability, prepaid, credit distribution, loyalty & consumer engagement. This allows Pine Labs to capture more economics around each transaction.

The third is Business Services, Data & AI - analytics, fraud, underwriting, identity, merchant intelligence & agentic commerce. Management highlights that industry profit pools are shifting from pure transaction processing towards higher value software, intelligence & automation.

If Pine Labs can sustain 20%+ REV growth (which is what the management is essentially guiding for) while continuing to shift mix towards higher margin products, operating leverage will continue to play out

Overall, Pine Labs is evolving from a payment acceptance company into a commerce infrastructure platform

items.title: Ratnamani just won a big order for spooling business. What differentiates spooling vs normal piping business? -Plain pipe is a spread business on a pa...
items.description_html:
Ratnamani just won a big order for spooling business.

What differentiates spooling vs normal piping business?

-Plain pipe is a spread business on a pass-through. Price per tonne is roughly steel cost plus a conversion charge. Steel is 65–75% of the selling price and moves with HRC/plate/billet indices, so the mill's real economics are a thin conversion spread sitting on top of a large pass-through base.

-Two consequences: (a) the margin percentage is arithmetically compressed because the denominator is inflated by material the mill never really "owned" economically, and (b) the product is fungible — once two mills are on the same approved vendor list for API 5L X65, the buyer runs a reverse auction and price converges to the marginal supplier's cost plus a sliver.

Spooling sells something else entirely: avoided site work.

-A spool is pipe cut to isometric drawings, welded to elbows, tees, reducers and flanges, radiographed, hydro-tested, PWHT'd where needed, coated, tagged, and shipped as a numbered assembly that gets bolted or tied in at site. What the customer is buying is the elimination of field welds.

-That's where the margin comes from, and it's the key first principle: your margin is set by the gap between your cost to do the work and the customer's cost to do it themselves. Shop welding with positioners, jigs and automated processes runs several times more productive per joint than field welding.

-Do that same weld on an offshore platform or inside a live refinery during a turnaround, and you're paying for scaffolding, access, hot-work permits, weather windows, vessel or barge day-rates, and the big one is deferred production for every day the shutdown runs long. The client's alternative cost is enormous, so willingness-to-pay is anchored to their avoided cost, not to your input cost. Pricing shifts from cost-plus to value-based.

Thus, in recent quarterly result. Ratnamani generated nearly 52% EBITDA MARGINS from the spooling division.

Disc: no recommendation to buy or sell.

items.title: This is a very interesting timeline. For the period under study, the most telling are the changes in size of the British military. Despite ruling the ...
items.description_html:
This is a very interesting timeline. For the period under study, the most telling are the changes in size of the British military. Despite ruling the world's largest empire, it had only the 4th-5th largest military in the world except during major conflicts. It was usually the best trained and armed force, but not the largest. Three things allowed this relatively small force to rule a large empire (1) mobility - hence the importance of a navy, it could turn up where it was needed; (2) a mass mobilisation and training system that allowed rapid expansion when needed; (3) the British Indian army that could deployed from Africa, China or even Europe. The last is not adequately emphasized. Once the loyalty of this force came into question, the empire fell apart within a generation.

items.title: RT Ben Judah: This is very real. Britain has a serious intellectual and policy China weakness. This is especially a problem in the Foreign Office. Bey...
items.description_html:
RT Ben Judah
This is very real. Britain has a serious intellectual and policy China weakness.

This is especially a problem in the Foreign Office. Beyond summitry and crisis management which the office does well, the institution remains excellent at our traditional friends (G7, Canada, Australia) and our traditional enemy (Russia) but with the exception of India is very weak on countries that fall in between. Shockingly to me that includes China where the overall intellectual and policy quality in King Charles Street is sadly very low.

There is nothing like what Jake Sullivan built up in DC: a network of experts and new capacity that are not China-country experts per se but expert on the intersection between China and global trends from tech to supply lines and specific nodes of manufacturing.

There is also nothing like China House which Tony Blinken built up in the State Department: a China expert hub that built up this up in house and exposed the Secretary of State to debates and challenges stemming from China’s global impact not uniquely in the bilateral frame.

What I found myself being served up was China, not every day, but China occasionally, effectively as it came up in bilateral ties. However this is rare as we don’t have a richly summited relationship with Beijing like with our other essential relationships. The viewpoint in house felt very much “Hong Kong 2010” and totally disconnected from European, Indian and American policy debates about China.

This isn’t entirely the FCDO’s fault. It reflects a British weakness. The London China analysis scene and China debate is thin, siloed and small. It doesn’t infuse the national debate. This is in sharp contrast to the British Russia debate, which is deep and rich and enriches Parliament and the media with real knowledge about Russia. Head and shoulders above France or Germany by far.

This isn’t going to solve itself on its own. It’s also not something I think government can fix on its own. What we need is a group of major philanthropists to come together with government to build our China knowledge infrastructure for the 21st century. And no, this isn’t the kind of suggestion the Cabinet Office will come up with like “hire 12 Mandarin speakers on SCS3 level.” This should be a generational project with Victorian ambition about it to enable the country to read this new world based off a significant university-scale endowment.

We should be building up our China intellectual infrastructure like we did with Russian Studies at the start of the Cold War. What we need at a minimum is a highly funded and prestigious, densely connected network made up of serious think tanks, university programs, numerous fellowships, extensive school and university language programs, libraries, diplomatic and wider civil service career streams, exchanges, cultural initiatives, changes and new requirements for the BBC and public funded broadcasting and translation services.

We need to know as a country, in our national debate, both what policies individual Chinese cities, universities and companies are doing well on engineering, science, tech and AI deployment we might want to adopt and also what the huge risks are to our economy and security.

Given China is ahead across most scientific-engineering domains and engaging in the largest military build up in human history, we have no choice. Now the alternative, of course, unless we build this, is sub-contracting our China thinking to our American or European allies who are doing this with quite different interests or overly relying on Chinese and Hong Kong diasporas now established in London, again with a particular slant.


Sander Tordoir: Indeed.

I see little understanding of China shock 2.0 amongst British officials, much less policy ideas.

There may also not be a willingness to act as China is still seen as a growth market in London - a vintage perspective that may well age poorly.

items.description_html:
RT Sonal Varma
Beyond the headlines, AI has added jobs in Asia—so far.

Our research finds 131,000 documented AI-related hires, compared with 61,000 job losses. But the headline numbers conceal an increasingly uneven impact:

• Job losses are concentrated in financial services and routine, lower-skilled technology roles.

• More than 90% of new jobs are in the technology sector, particularly AI training, data annotation and data operations.

• AI is creating a K-shaped labour market: entry-level hiring is weakening, while demand for experienced talent is rising.

• India is ground zero for this disruption because of its large IT and back-office sector. The net impact has been positive so far, but reduced campus recruitment represents a less visible form of displacement. @Nomura

https://www.nomuraconnects.com/focused-thinking-posts/beyond-the-headlines-ai-has-added-jobs-in-asia-so-far/

items.title: Just read the following Para carefully from Nephrocare's concall and understand why Dialysis is a difficult business to be profitable at. Dialysis loo...
items.description_html:
Just read the following Para carefully from Nephrocare's concall and understand why Dialysis is a difficult business to be profitable at.

Dialysis looks like a wonderful business on paper i.e. recurring revenue, non-discretionary demand, a patient who comes back three times a week for years. NephroPlus is the cleanest Indian case study for why it isn't, and the numbers are unusually honest about it.

1. You don't set the price. The payer does.

This is the root problem. Dialysis pricing in India runs around $22–25 per session, while the Philippines operates at roughly $110 per treatment for the identical clinical procedure, same machine, same consumables, 4–5x the realisation. That gap has nothing to do with cost or quality; it reflects what the payer can afford. In India the payer is largely the government (PPP tenders), insurance schemes, or a price-sensitive self-payer. You bid for volume in a tender; you don't price to value.

Watch how NephroPlus actually improved its realisation: blended RPT rose 13.3% in FY26 to ₹2,598, and 9.2% in Q1FY27 to ₹2,733. But that's mix, not pricing power as international went from 12% of revenue in FY23 to ~41% in 9MFY26 and 45% by Q1FY27. The company fixed its unit economics by leaving India, not by winning in it.

2. Cost per session is fixed, imported, and non-negotiable.

Dialyzer, tubing, dialysate, needles, EPO, plus nurse and technician time, every session consumes roughly the same basket. Machines and RO plants are largely imported. So you have a capped price and a floor on variable cost. Gross margin per session is structurally thin, and the only lever left is utilisation.

3. Utilisation is the whole game, but geography fights you.

Management says it plainly: dialysis is fundamentally a scale-driven business where higher volume drives operating leverage, asset utilisation and ROCE. But dialysis is a four-hour treatment required multiple times a week, which makes proximity critical as over 75% of NephroPlus's Indian clinics sit in tier-2 and tier-3 cities. Patients won't travel, so you must build small clinics close to them. Small clinics mean few machines, and a machine either runs its three shifts or it doesn't. Breakeven is a step function, not a curve. A greenfield clinic takes about 12 months to reach operational breakeven versus 3–4 months for an acquired one — so every year of expansion carries a drag cohort.

4. The financial history is the evidence.

Founded 2009–10. Raised roughly $205M across 13 rounds from 33 investors. For first 11 years of its life, Nephro was EBITDA negative and for 13 years it was PAT negative. High fixed cost businesses need massive scale to generate margins.

Disclaimer: no recommendation to buy or sell. Concall summary from @stockscansin

Homer's Guide to the Galaxy - Shruti Rajagopalan

TL,DR // Douglas Adams says the fjords of Norway were designed by a man called Slartibartfast, and his work won an award. Shruti Rajagopalan saw Hjørundfjorden last week and agrees the award was well deserved. She argues The Hitchhiker's Guide is The Odyssey retold.

Odysseus had a home to return to, and that homecoming made his tale one of the most retold stories we have. Arthur Dent watched his home get demolished in chapter one. Homer invents gods to explain why the cleverest man alive needs ten years to sail home. Adams invents the Infinite Improbability Drive to explain why the most ordinary man in the galaxy keeps surviving.

I'll admit I can't tell you what the essay adds up to, but it's well worth the ride (er, read).

items.title: RT Michael Pettis: But what a depressingly large number of economists don't understand is that exchange rate adjustments do alter the saving/investmen...
items.description_html:
RT Michael Pettis
But what a depressingly large number of economists don't understand is that exchange rate adjustments do alter the saving/investment balance. They effectively shift income between consumers of tradable goods and producers of tradable goods. An appreciation, for example, puts downward pressure on saving by shifting income from net producers (e.g. manufacturers) to net consumers (the household sector), thereby rasing the consumption share of GDP.

In his 2008 paper, “The Real Exchange Rate and Economic Growth”, Dani Rodrik makes this point, arguing that a real depreciation is equivalent to a production subsidy plus a consumption tax on tradables. He then says that directly subsidizing tradable production would achieve the production-supporting effect without the consumption-tax effect.

And it's not just Rodrik. Almost everybody used to know this. In his 1944 book, Ragnar Nurkse said that “the devaluation of a currency is expansionary in effect if it corrects a previous overvaluation, but deflationary if it makes the currency undervalued.” He was making the same argument -- if saving is too low, devaluation expands production, and if it is too high, it weakens production.

Perhaps most famously, in his classic 1965 work on Argentina, Carlos Díaz Alejandro emphasized the redistribution caused by devaluation. A devaluation raises the domestic prices of tradable goods, reducing the real purchasing power of workers and consumers while benefiting producers and exporters. Because different groups have different propensities to consume and save, he explained, the redistribution can have major effects on aggregate demand and saving.

Peter Montiel in 2000 and Montiel and Servén in 2008 said the same thing, arguing that an undervalued currency changes intertemporal relative prices, discouraging consumption in favor of saving and making investment in tradables relatively more attractive than investment in non-tradables. Consequently, when the currency eventually appreciates, consumption rises and investment shifts toward non-tradables.

This is hardly a new idea. More generally, the distinction between policies that are intended to change an external imbalance and policies that are intended to change an internal imbalance is a spurious one. You cannot change one without the other, and either policy works by changing the saving/investment balance.

items.title: What is Terminal value of a business? When you value a business, you can only forecast a few years properly. But businesses don't stop at year five. T...
items.description_html:
What is Terminal value of a business?

When you value a business, you can only forecast a few years properly. But businesses don't stop at year five. Terminal value is the shorthand for everything that happens after your forecast ends.

Put simply: terminal value is the market's assumption that the business will still be here, still profitable, still earning more than its cost of capital, long after anyone can meaningfully forecast it.

And it is the majority of what you pay for. Most of the value in any long-duration business sits beyond the years you can actually model.

So when you buy something at a high multiple, you are not really expressing a view on next year's profit. You are expressing a view on whether this business still matters in twenty years.

Why PE de-rates the moment terminal value is in doubt

A PE multiple is a duration measure disguised as a price measure. A high multiple means the market expects the cash flows to keep coming for a very long time. A low multiple means it doesn't.

So when durability comes into question, three things happen:

The largest component of value is the one being questioned. Near-term earnings are the small part. The forever part is the big part. Doubt the forever part and you have doubted most of the valuation at once, even though the P&L hasn't changed a line.

The market doesn't wait for proof. It doesn't need the business to die. It only needs to become less sure that it lives. Moving from certainty to doubt is enough, because a large number multiplied by lower confidence is a much smaller number. That is why the de-rate arrives on the first credible threat, not on the eventual outcome.

The multiple falls back to what a business with no future is worth. Everything a stock trades above a plain, no-growth valuation is payment for longevity. Remove the belief in longevity and that premium has nothing holding it up.

The stock doesn't drift down. It resets to the floor. If the market thinks the business is actually shrinking, it goes below the floor, which is what those optically cheap, obviously-declining names are really telling you.

Few examples below includes:

Radiant: Threat of UPI & Cashless economy
CMS : Thread of UPI & cashless economy
IEX: Threat of coupling to terminal value

items.title: Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles. A key q...
items.description_html:
Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles.

A key question is — if the existing sponsor capital has already increased by nearly 20% in the last year, why does the company need to raise fresh capital from public investors to invest further in these high-risk, illiquid assets?

Interestingly, around 85% of Gaja’s income comes from management fees and carried interest, while income from sponsor commitments contributes only about 10%.

This raises a fundamental question: a significant portion of the fresh issue proceeds is being deployed toward an activity that currently contributes a relatively small share of revenue.

Moreover, carried interest is dependent on successful exits and realisation of investment gains. Until portfolio investments are monetised, the carried interest recorded in financial statements may not necessarily translate into actual cash inflows.

The key investor question is whether the additional sponsor commitments will create enough incremental value through future fee income and carry generation to justify the capital being raised

items.title: Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20% The vaccine is not a prev...
items.description_html:
Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20%

The vaccine is not a preventive vaccine like a COVID shot. It's made after patient already has cancer. Each dose is built individually for that patient from the mutations found in their own tumour — you sequence the tumour, find the mutated proteins unique to it ("neoantigens"), and make an mRNA shot that teaches the immune system to hunt cells carrying those specific mutations.

It's the first proof the idea works. Neoantigen vaccines have been a theoretical hope in oncology for years, but this is the first randomised Phase 3 trial designed to definitively prove the benefit.

If the mechanism is real, it's platform technology — the same pipeline could in principle be pointed at lung, kidney, bladder cancers. One analyst noted the results also read positively for the vaccine's ongoing studies in other cancer types. That optionality is what "holy grail" headlines are reaching for.

items.title: The government has approved 31 more projects under ECMS, taking the total to 106 projects with ₹69,548 crore of planned investment. ECMS is basically...
items.description_html:
The government has approved 31 more projects under ECMS, taking the total to 106 projects with ₹69,548 crore of planned investment.

ECMS is basically India’s push to build the components that go inside electronics products, from connectors, capacitors, and camera modules to battery materials and optical transceivers.

The interesting part: 38 plants are already manufacturing, while another 16 are close to starting production.

India is slowly moving from “assembling electronics” to actually building the supply chain behind them. That shift could create a much bigger opportunity for domestic component manufacturers over the next few years.

Over the past five fiscals ending FY26, India has witnessed healthy growth in steel demand, largely led by the Government’s focus on boosting infrastructure development, resulting in robust demand across key end-user segments, including building & construction, transport infrastructure and automotive. This growth is mirrored in the expansion of domestic steel capacity, with major players investing heavily.

However, global consumption ex-India has continued to decline since CY21, and recovery in global demand faces significant headwinds, accentuated by geopolitical uncertainties from time to time. This has also led to trade tensions and concerns about cheaper steel imports, affecting the profitability of Indian manufacturers. That said, fluctuating raw material prices pose further challenges to domestic steel producers.

items.description_html:
🚨 C2C’s auditor has issued a qualified opinion and flagged multiple serious financial and compliance concerns:

1️⃣ Liquidity & Going Concern Risk:
The company is facing a liquidity crisis, with statutory dues unpaid due to lack of funds. Recovery from trade receivables remains uncertain, while operations are heavily dependent on short-term promoter funding. The auditor has raised doubt over C2C’s ability to continue as a going concern. Liquidation Risk

2️⃣ CSR Payments Not Cleared:
CSR expenses were recognised through cheques, creating a book overdraft. However, the cheques were not presented for payment. The auditor noted that the CSR obligation is discharged only when the payment is actually cleared.

3️⃣ Statutory Dues Pending:
Undisputed statutory payments remain unpaid. No provision has been made for possible interest or penalties. Delays in filing statutory returns and weak internal controls were also highlighted.

4️⃣ Labour Code Impact Not Assessed:
The company has not quantified the potential impact of new labour regulations on gratuity, provident fund, wages and other employee benefits.

5️⃣ FEMA Compliance Issues:
Overseas receivables remain unrealised beyond RBI timelines. Applications for regularisation are pending, SOFTEX registration is yet to be approved, and possible penalties have not been provided for.

items.title: RT Sridhar Vembu: Last week, I was fortunate to visit the workshop (the Tamil word pattarai பட்டறை is so appropriate) of the leading motor desig...
items.description_html:
RT Sridhar Vembu
Last week, I was fortunate to visit the workshop (the Tamil word pattarai பட்டறை is so appropriate) of the leading motor designer in the world Morihiro Saito-san.

Saito-san is 80+ and still designing advanced motors, some of the most advanced in the world. His modest looking workshop is right next door to a company that builds out those motors in prototype quantities and he works closely with them to get them built. I visited as an industrial "pilgrim", with as much devotion as I go to the Thoranamalai Murugan Temple at home. When I saw him at work, I was moved to touch his feet.

Saito-san, the God of motors, is how Japan is able to retain its global prominence in so many foundational industries.

We need to learn from that spirit. We need to revive our "pattarai" culture of building things - every village in India needs such workshops!

My industrial pilgrimage to Japan has given me new vigor 🙏

items.title: RT Sagar Awatade: I don't know who else to tell this to, so I am going to tell my story here. Every day is a struggle for a young business, but the la...
items.description_html:
RT Sagar Awatade
I don't know who else to tell this to, so I am going to tell my story here.

Every day is a struggle for a young business, but the last few months have been harder than usual.

We are a small Indian company. For more than ten years we have been building a homegrown brand in a product category dominated by big foreign players.

There are almost no Indian names in this space. We set out to be one.

We started in 2014. Over the years we began making parts in India instead of just importing, and we started selling in the US, Dubai, Nepal, Malaysia and South Africa.

We showed up at global trade fairs to represent an Indian brand on the world stage.

In 2023 we changed the import code we use for our product. We did not do this quietly. Every shipment was declared. Nothing was hidden. We didn't invent our approach.

We followed written professional advice and the way this product is treated in markets around the world.

And now we are facing a government demand running into tens of crores in duty recovery and penalties, plus personal penalties on the founders and even on an employee.

For a company our size, this is not a fine we can pay and move on from. This ends us.

We have not run from any of this. I am not built like that. It is not how I was raised. We have written to the authorities, met officials in person, and we have now filed a writ in the High Court.

All we are asking for is a fair treatment.

I set out to build in India and sell to the world. I am asking only that the system back honest founders trying to compete globally, instead of breaking them.

The process is the process, and it exists for a reason. But process should not feel like punishment.

From where I am standing today, it does.
I am not giving up. I have worked too hard for this. If you have read this far, please share it. If you know someone who can help, point them my way. Help me get the word out.

items.description_html: Agentic routing is such an interesting study. Built a basic agent that does planning on Opus 4 but reasons on 4.6 through a tool call (skill call). Due to lack of document grounding, I embedded corpus into system prompt. Worked well. Second stage, enabled managed RAG for grounding & agent stated skipping tool call entirely, no skill calls. It treated grounded data as a higher evidence deterministic choice & skipped skill call. Tweaked tool description, still no skill call. Changed skill description matching to tool call & bingo!! Agent skipped grounding, entered planning mode & made a tool call. Evals for Agentic behavior is literally out paces everything in this field. What's your such key learning from a recent build?

items.title: A lot of defense to IT SIs right now is based on assumption that enterprise clients will not open their systems, data & processes to external AI solut...
items.description_html: A lot of defense to IT SIs right now is based on assumption that enterprise clients will not open their systems, data & processes to external AI solutions (Claude, OpenAi). However, this defense collapses the moment we have a precedence from a big enterprise opening up just the way enterprises opened up to cloud after a decade long friction. The moment this starts happening, the JVs OpenAi & Claude have formed will make a killing. And, what will take this wall down? For e.g., enterprises are currently very upset after SAP API policy that prohibited clients from using their own data & sending it to external tools via APIs to architect a solution outside of SAP. This can be the 1st hammer in the wall. One wrong step & clients will find ways to disconnect with enterprise OEMs & will be willing to trust(with an agreement perhaps) likes of Claude & OpenAi. The moment this happens, it is done!! This is the biggest risk I foresee.

items.title: Exactly 10 years ago in May 2016, i went to a session on bootstrapping at TiE event in Santa Clara. That changed my life. When i spent time in bay are...
items.description_html:
Exactly 10 years ago in May 2016, i went to a session on bootstrapping at TiE event in Santa Clara. That changed my life.

When i spent time in bay area working on advanced sensing technologies in semicon space, everything was there in life(money, granted patents, travelling to new country every month, wife, so called good life) but it still felt empty within.

Was burning a lot of midnight oil trying to build something, failed twice trying to build in US. Those failures hit hard and made me realise that everthing that i had was only beacuse of the company that i was working for, i was zero outside of it.

During this phase is when i first met @svembu ji, did not know who he was, did not know about zoho. He was wearing a plain simple green kurtha, jeans and slippers gving a session on bootstraping his company. I asked "can we bootstrap a hardware business too ?" And he said " why not ? "

This along with zoho story, made my conviction of moving back to India stronger, it took almost a week for me to digest what zoho was and what was built without raising a single dime from VCs and i felt so proud and blessed to have met the man behind.

Moved back to India same year in October. It was only about building something here which makes sense in long term, something which was ignored by people for a long time.

Ofcourse it came at a cost, divorce, hard time telling people not to worry about me or my personal life, making sure that my parents are not suffering, isolating all the peronal stuff with the vision of building strong electronics manufacutring ecosystem in India.

10 years FF- we are a strong team of 200+, bootstrapped, growing fast, building factories in India which can compete globally soon. On a personal level, i still hardly spend few thousand rupess everymonth, lead a minimal life, have a loving wife who belives in me and a kid who is growing fast, parents who are proud that i am doing something in India.

There is no multimillion dollars in my bank as safety, my kid and wife are Indians with Indian passport and my parents were teachers/avg govt employee without any background in business.

I dont feel empty inside me, anymore. Fire inside me is for building India's electronics manufacturing capacity that can compete globally, a strong ecosystem for next gen to build products from India and a strong team that can run this beyond me.

Jai Hind!🇮🇳

items.title: P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/E...
items.description_html:
P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. I had demonstrated this through correlation analysis in an earlier investor memo.

The chart below tracks the P/B ratio (blue line) of the Nifty Smallcap 100 Index against the 25th percentile of its trailing 5-year P/B range (orange line). In simple terms, when the blue line falls below the orange line, the current valuation is in the lowest quartile of the past five years.

Since P/B is broadly proportional to ROE, the structural improvement in index ROE—from ~8–12% in the previous decade to ~15% currently—has led to a gradual upward shift in the orange line over time.

Notably, for the first time since the COVID crash, the current P/B has moved below this 25th percentile threshold. Historically, similar instances—during the 2011–2013 downturn, Q1 2016 correction, and the COVID crash—have been followed by strong returns over the subsequent 1–3 years.

This does not imply that markets have bottomed, nor does it guarantee short-term gains. In an event-driven environment, especially with geopolitical risks such as an escalation in war, markets could decline further by 10–20%.

However, what can be said with a reasonably high degree of confidence is that forward-looking returns over a 1–3 year horizon from such valuation levels have historically been better than average.

items.title: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely...
items.description_html: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely rare to see the Mid & Small cap indices (avg of the two) beating the Nifty 50 near the bottom of the cycle. Their avg CAGR has outperformed during the last two tough years as well as all the below trailing years. I am not that surprised as their balance sheet, P&L and cash flow quality has substantially improved post COVID. I believe the biggest multi-baggers will emerge from this space as the earnings growth differential will be significant going forward. Because of the quality differential today vs during pre-COVID period, I would be surprised if their valuations correct to levels seen during the previous crashes. We probably have the best corporate quality and least stressed financials currently compared to any other previous big crisis.

items.title: As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/Mar...
items.description_html:
As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/March trough—are not an exception; they are a recurring feature of market cycles. Just as consistently, these phases have been followed by sharp recoveries once the market establishes a bottom in February or March.
Current sentiment is such that investors are overly focused on the negatives, making the environment appear so foggy that positives have become invisible. This fog, as always, will eventually lift.

While market bottoms and the depth of drawdowns can never be predicted, it is highly probable that market levels a few months from now will be disproportionately higher. Unfortunately, short-term declines are unsettling for investors, causing many to step aside and miss the eventual strong upswing.

In hindsight, this phase will look like an obvious opportunity. But while living through it, investors see only risks and landmines—never the runway for the next flight
